doc.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023

title: Mose Allison singing at the piano; Sidran as his producer
summary: Frishberg and Allison write to their vocal limits; Sidran produced six Allison records with no overdubs.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: It reminds me of, I had a conversation with Dave Frishberg and he said, “When I write I’m writing according to the limitations of my own vocal ability.” And then he said, “I bet Mose Allison would say the same thing. A lot of his songs are shaped by the way he sings.”

Yeah. I think that’s true. I know Mose also believed that he had to be playing piano in order to sing, that they were of one piece. You had to be sitting at the piano and accompanying himself when he sang.

Did that make it harder to — harder is not the right word — but often times, as you well know, vocals are overdubbed and you have more control over it so if he’s playing the piano at the same time it’s just another task for the engineer I guess.

You know I was his producer for a while, I produced six records for him. And he didn’t overdub anything. Everything was captured. Nothing was manufactured. But if you listen to his early recordings, you know he tends to make kind of grunting sounds when he’s improvising, a lot of jazz musicians do. But on his first records the engineer could have muted his vocal mic during his solos but didn’t. And he was treated harshly that way because the records would come out and you could hear him. And reviewers commented on it. So there is a responsibility from the engineer but generally speaking for Mose it was one thing, it really — he was not going to separate it out.
